title: Inexact bilevel stochastic gradient methods for constrained and unconstrained lower-level problems
contribution: A bilevel stochastic gradient (BSG) framework for lower levels that are unconstrained or have nonlinear, possibly nonconvex constraints (via the LL KKT Jacobian). Its SG convergence theory (nonconvex, strongly convex 1/k, convex 1/sqrt(k)) covers every kind of inexactness: inexact LL solve, inexact adjoint solve or truncated Neumann series, and noisy derivatives. Two Hessian-free practical methods, BSG-N-FD and BSG-1, come with released code.
problem_entry: ML applications (continual learning, NAS, adversarial training, hyperparameter tuning), plus an uncovered class: prior BSG work handles only unconstrained LLs, or constraints that are linear or depend only on y. A third factor is the cost of second-order and Neumann-series information (pp. 3-5).
key_idea: Apply SG to f(x) = f_u(x, y(x)) with an inexact adjoint gradient d(D) = -(a - A B^-1 b). A constrained LL only changes B (the Hessian becomes the KKT Jacobian under LICQ/SCS/SOSC), so one analysis covers the constrained/unconstrained and deterministic/stochastic cases. Every error source is budgeted at O(alpha_k) (pp. 7-15).
assumptions: Lipschitz and bounded derivatives and stochastic estimates. A strongly convex LL (unconstrained case) or LICQ+SCS+SOSC with bounded inverse KKT matrices (constrained case). Bounded second moment. A sensitivity (Lipschitz-in-data) assumption, called 'not restrictive'. LL error, sampling error and residual all O(alpha_k). Robbins-Monro steps. Strongly convex and convex f are admitted to be impractical (pp. 10-20).
proof_devices: sensitivity of d(D) = -(a - A B^-1 b) from three facts: sums Lipschitz, products of bounded factors Lipschitz, inverses with singular values bounded away from zero Lipschitz (Prop. 3.1, p. 13; App. A pp. 42-43)
error budget: E||w(x_k) - w~_k||^2 <= (C_w alpha_k)^2, sampling error <= C_D alpha_k, residual <= C_e alpha_k => direction bias <= C_d alpha_k (Lemma 3.2, p. 15)
descent lemma with the bias at order alpha_k^2: E f(x_{k+1}) - f(x_k) <= -alpha_k ||P_X grad f||^2 + alpha_k^2 C C_d + 0.5 alpha_k^2 L G_d (Lemma 4.2, p. 17)
Bottou-Curtis-Nocedal Thm 4.10 argument with sum alpha = inf, sum alpha^2 < inf (Thm 4.3, p. 18); O(1/k) strongly convex (Thm 4.4, p. 19); O(1/sqrt k) convex (Thm 4.5, p. 20)
enforcement recipes: i_k = k^2 inner SG steps with beta_i = gamma/i (p. 20); mini-batch sizes growing as alpha_k shrinks, with Gaussian estimates (p. 21)
implicit-function/KKT sensitivity for a constrained LL: grad y = -grad_x G grad_v G^-1 L (2.7) (p. 7)
experiments: Python code on GitHub, 10 seeds. Synthetic quadratic bilevel problem (n = m = 300), with an unconstrained LL, 50 linear constraints, or 5 quadratic constraints. Baselines: DARTS, StocBiO, SIGD; none exist for quadratic constraints. CIFAR-10 continual learning with and without GEM-style LL constraints. Metrics: UL iterations and time. Per-algorithm step-size grids. Failures to tune are reported. There is no collection, no profiles and no UL constraint (pp. 22-36).
positioning: Critiques prior BSG work by the restrictive assumptions each needs (solve to optimality, Neumann ||H|| < 1, linear constraints only). Claims to unify the adjoint-equation and Neumann classes and to generalize 'all existing approaches'. Built on the Bottou-Curtis-Nocedal SG theory and on Fiacco/McCormick sensitivity. Only 2 of 66 references are self-citations (pp. 4-5, 8, 10, 37-41).
writing: A numbered first/second-main-contribution paragraph with first-of-kind claims (pp. 5, 30, 36). Each assumption gets a purpose sentence, and strong assumptions are admitted where they appear (pp. 19-20). Sparse hedging ('seem to'). Long proofs are in the appendices (pp. 42-45).
limits_future: Written: strongly convex/convex regimes impractical; BSG-1 has no theory; slightly slower in time on continual learning. Not written: step-size and FD-parameter mismatch with the theory, no total-work count, no UL-constrained test. Future: NAS with LL constraints, variance reduction (pp. 5, 19-20, 37).

title: A stochastic gradient method for trilevel optimization
contribution: The first stochastic gradient method for unconstrained-ML/LL trilevel problems (TSG). It has a nonconvex rate O(J/sqrt(I)) under K >= O(J^3 I), and the analysis covers inexact ML/LL solves, inexact adjoint computation and noisy derivatives up to third order. Also: Hessian-free variants (TSG-N-FD, TSG-AD), a trilevel formulation of adversarial hyperparameter tuning, and code.
problem_entry: Extend the bilevel SG toolkit one level down for ML uses. The gap is that no stochastic trilevel method exists: prior work either lacks guarantees (evolutionary), lacks numerics (proximal), or is deterministic (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Eliminate one level at a time through the solution maps (TLO -> BLO -> single level). The trilevel adjoint gradient is the classical adjoint applied to the reduced bilevel problem. Run three nested warm-started SG loops, with a composite step theta = alpha*beta*gamma that scales all bias assumptions (pp. 2-6).
assumptions: f1 C1, f2 C2, f3 C3, with f1, grad f1, f2, grad f2, Hess f2, grad f3, Hess f3, third-order tensor of f3 all Lipschitz. f3 strongly convex in z and f-bar strongly convex in y. Unbiased i.i.d. bounded-variance estimates. Bounded inverse stochastic Hessians with O(theta) bias. Strong convexity is admitted as the main limitation (pp. 5-6, 9).
proof_devices: Lyapunov V = f(x) + ||y - y(x)||^2 + ||z - z(x)||^2 + ||z - z(x,y)||^2, chosen only for telescoping (B.1, p. 14)
one lemma per Lyapunov difference: UL descent with bias and coupling terms; LL contraction (1 - gamma rho)^K and ^{JK}; auxiliary LL error; ML contraction (1 - psi beta)^J (Lemmas B.1-B.4, p. 16)
SGD contraction on a strongly convex function via Nesterov Thm 2.1.12, applied by induction over K and J (App. C.2, pp. 17-18)
bias of the UL/ML directions O(theta) and bounded second moments (Lemmas D.3-D.6, App. D pp. 31-41)
coefficient-sign analysis (A1 >= 0, A2-A4 <= 0) yielding the loop-length conditions K >= Xi(I,J) = O(J^3 I), then telescoping (App. C.5, pp. 26-30)
experiments: Code on GitHub. Synthetic quadratic (n = m = t = 50) and quartic (n = m = 5, t = 1) problems with Gaussian noise; 95% t-intervals over 10 runs; hand-picked decaying steps. Adversarial hyperparameter tuning on wine and California housing data, measured by test MSE under feature noise over 100 draws. Comparators are the bilevel formulations obtained by dropping a level, plus the level-swapped formulation of prior work; there is no external trilevel algorithm (pp. 7-9, 44-47).
positioning: Claims the first stochastic trilevel method. Sorts prior work by the missing ingredient (guarantees / numerics / stochasticity). Adapts Chen-Sun-Yin's bilevel analysis and benchmarks the rate against it. Disagrees with Sato et al.'s level ordering and tests both. Self-citations: S042, S070, the 1994 bibliography (pp. 1-2, 6, 8, 15, 47).
writing: 'first-ever' in the abstract. The main theorem is stated in its implementable form and the sharper rate is a remark. A post-theorem paragraph reads K >= O(J^3 I) as upward error propagation across levels and ends with an open question. A specific 'Potential limitations' paragraph. 35 of 47 pages are appendices (pp. 1, 6, 9, 13-47).
limits_future: Written: strong convexity at ML/LL; bilevel formulations competitive in runtime; only tabular regression. Future: accuracy relations across levels, penalization for nonconvex lower levels. Not written: no total oracle count; experimental steps differ from the theorem's; quartic test problem violates Assumption 3.2; sharper rate and Lipschitz proofs only in an unpublished thesis (pp. 6, 9, 41, 45).

quotes.text: Such a relationship underscores how errors in the LL propagate upward through the levels: greater accuracy at any sub-upper level necessitates significantly higher precision in the LL solution.
Potential limitations of our work include the strong convexity assumptions on the ML and LL objective functions, which constrain the applicability of our TSG method.
